title: Sariputra transformed
hookLine: the goddess switches bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed

cards: Shariputra is still sitting there with petals on his robe, and he has a question for the goddess. She's clearly wise; she's just out-talked him about the flowers. So he asks: why don't you change out of your female form?

Some readers hear behind it an old view that certain attainments weren't open to a woman as a woman. To him, the question sounds reasonable. The goddess answers it twice: once with words, and once with his own body.

teach.h: I'VE LOOKED, AND FOUND NO MARKS.
teach.b: First the words, paraphrased. I've looked for the marks of being female, she says, and I haven't found them. So what would I change?
Suppose a magician conjures up a woman.
Would you ask the illusion to change her form? No, says Shariputra; an illusion has no fixed form to change. Just so, says the goddess.
Nothing has a fixed form. Then the second answer. By her power, she turns Shariputra into a likeness of herself, and herself into a likeness of Shariputra.
Now the goddess, in his form, asks Shariputra, in hers: why don't you change out of your female form?

teach.h: I DON'T KNOW HOW I TURNED INTO THIS.
teach.b: Bewildered, he answers: I don't know how I turned into this. If you could change out of it, she says, then everyone in a woman's form could change. You aren't a woman, yet you appear as one.
In the same way, all who appear as women aren't women in some fixed, final way.
The Buddha taught that all things are neither male nor female. Then she lets him go back. Where is your female form now, she asks.

It isn't anywhere, and it isn't nowhere, says Shariputra. That's how it is with all things, she says. Afterward Vimalakirti tells him this goddess has served many Buddhas and can take whatever birth she wishes.
A few weeks ago, the Lotus had the dragon king's daughter changing form to make a point. Here the question is turned around on the one asking it.
The label he was sure of turns out not to be fixed.

how: Mahayana teachers read the goddess's exchange with Shariputra as a lesson on emptiness, that no form is fixed, and some modern Buddhist writers also draw on it in discussions of women in Buddhism.

o: a disciple reborn as a goddess for breaking a monk's rule
Shariputra and the goddess swap forms to show none is fixed
a monk who chooses to be reborn a woman to earn more merit

has no fixed form to change

games.q: you're Shariputra. the goddess has turned you into her likeness and asks why you don't change out of your female form. what do you say?
o: I don't know how I turned into this.
this was never my real body.
games.why: he's bewildered, and the goddess answers: you aren't a woman, yet you appear as one; so it is with all who appear as women.

practice: Bring to mind a label you wear, or one you've put on someone: the shy one, the difficult one, too old for that. Ask what the goddess asked: where exactly is it?
Look for where it begins and ends, and notice whether it's as solid as it sounded.

wordCard.voice: Sariputra transformed. The goddess swaps forms with him to show that male and female aren't fixed, and asks why he doesn't change back. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: emptiness, the teaching behind the goddess's answer that no form is fixed.

carryVoice: Your line: not fixed. Even the one asking the question can change shape. Same time tomorrow.
